claim: Animal circadian rhythms persist in constant darkness.
source: Animal circadian rhythms persist in constant darkness and are driven by intracellular transcription-translation feedback loops.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Animal circadian rhythms are driven by intracellular transcription-translation feedback loops.
source: Animal circadian rhythms persist in constant darkness and are driven by intracellular transcription-translation feedback loops.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Isolated mammalian cellular clocks continue to tick away in darkness without intercellular communication.
source: Although these cellular oscillators communicate, isolated mammalian cellular clocks continue to tick away in darkness without intercellular communication.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian systems.

claim: Loss of the clock within both key clock neuron regions but neither one alone has a strong behavioral phenotype in darkness.
source: The results point to two key clock neuron groups: loss of the clock within both regions but neither one alone has a strong behavioral phenotype in darkness; communication between these regions also contributes to circadian period determination.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CRISPR knockout experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Communication between key clock neuron regions contributes to circadian period determination.
source: The results point to two key clock neuron groups: loss of the clock within both regions but neither one alone has a strong behavioral phenotype in darkness; communication between these regions also contributes to circadian period determination.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The clock within one region persists without network communication under dark conditions.
source: Under these dark conditions, the clock within one region persists without network communication.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the silencing experiments showing LNds maintain cycling.

claim: The clock within PDF-expressing s-LNv neurons was strongly dependent on network communication.
source: The clock within the famous PDF-expressing s-LNv neurons however was strongly dependent on network communication, likely because clock gene expression within these vulnerable sLNvs depends on neuronal firing or light.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the silencing experiments showing sLNvs dampen rapidly.

claim: Clock gene expression within sLNvs depends on neuronal firing or light.
source: The clock within the famous PDF-expressing s-LNv neurons however was strongly dependent on network communication, likely because clock gene expression within these vulnerable sLNvs depends on neuronal firing or light.
evidence: This is inferred from the tim mRNA data showing reduced levels upon silencing.

claim: The suprachiasmatic nucleus in mammals is composed of thousands of cells depending on the species.
source: The comparable region in mammals, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, is composed of thousands of cells depending on the species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian circadian systems.

claim: There are only 75 clock neurons per hemisphere in Drosophila.
source: There are in contrast only 75 clock neurons per hemisphere in Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila circadian systems.

claim: Drosophila clock neurons can be divided into several subgroups according to their location within the fly brain.
source: These different clock neurons can be divided into several subgroups according to their location within the fly brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Drosophila clock neuron organization.

claim: There are 4 lateral and three dorsal neuron clusters in Drosophila.
source: There are 4 lateral and three dorsal neuron clusters, which have different functions in controlling fly physiology (Helfrich-Förster et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Different clock neuron clusters have different functions in controlling fly physiology.
source: There are 4 lateral and three dorsal neuron clusters, which have different functions in controlling fly physiology (Helfrich-Förster et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The four small ventro-lateral neurons (sLNvs) are arguably the most important of the 75 clock neurons.
source: The four small ventro-lateral neurons (sLNvs) are arguably the most important of the 75 clock neurons.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: Ablating or silencing sLNvs abolishes rhythms in constant darkness.
source: This is because ablating or silencing these neurons abolishes rhythms in constant darkness (DD).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: sLNvs reside in the accessory medulla region of the fly brain.
source: They reside in the accessory medulla region of the fly brain, an important pacemaker center in many insects (Helfrich-Förster, 1997), and express the neuropeptide PDF.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The accessory medulla is an important pacemaker center in many insects.
source: They reside in the accessory medulla region of the fly brain, an important pacemaker center in many insects (Helfrich-Förster, 1997), and express the neuropeptide PDF.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: sLNvs express the neuropeptide PDF.
source: They reside in the accessory medulla region of the fly brain, an important pacemaker center in many insects (Helfrich-Förster, 1997), and express the neuropeptide PDF.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: sLNvs are essential for predicting dawn.
source: In addition, they are essential for predicting dawn (Depetris-Chauvin et al., 2011; Grima et al., 2004; Nitabach et al., 2002; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: sLNvs are able to modulate the timing of the evening peak of behavior via PDF.
source: A very recent study suggests that the sLNvs are also able to modulate the timing of the evening (E) peak of behavior via PDF (Renn et al., 1999; Schlichting et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: The four large-ventro-lateral neurons (lLNvs) also express PDF.
source: The other ventral-lateral group, the four large-ventro-lateral neurons (lLNvs), also express PDF and send projections to the medulla, the visual center of the fly brain; they are important arousal neurons (Shang et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: lLNvs send projections to the medulla, the visual center of the fly brain.
source: The other ventral-lateral group, the four large-ventro-lateral neurons (lLNvs), also express PDF and send projections to the medulla, the visual center of the fly brain; they are important arousal neurons (Shang et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: lLNvs are important arousal neurons.
source: The other ventral-lateral group, the four large-ventro-lateral neurons (lLNvs), also express PDF and send projections to the medulla, the visual center of the fly brain; they are important arousal neurons (Shang et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The absence of pdf function causes substantial arrhythmic behavior in DD.
source: Consistent with the ablation experiments mentioned above, the absence of pdf function or reducing PDF levels via RNAi causes substantial arrhythmic behavior in DD (Renn et al., 1999; Shafer and Taghert, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Reducing PDF levels via RNAi causes substantial arrhythmic behavior in DD.
source: Consistent with the ablation experiments mentioned above, the absence of pdf function or reducing PDF levels via RNAi causes substantial arrhythmic behavior in DD (Renn et al., 1999; Shafer and Taghert, 2009).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The dorso-lateral neurons (LNds) are essential for the timing of the E peak.
source: Other important clock neurons include the dorso-lateral neurons (LNds), which are essential for the timing of the E peak and adjustment to long photoperiods (Grima et al., 2004; Kistenpfennig et al., 2018; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: LNds are essential for adjustment to long photoperiods.
source: Other important clock neurons include the dorso-lateral neurons (LNds), which are essential for the timing of the E peak and adjustment to long photoperiods (Grima et al., 2004; Kistenpfennig et al., 2018; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The lateral-posterior neurons (LPN) and a subset of the dorsal neurons (DN1s) connect the clock network to sleep centers in the fly central complex.
source: Two other clock neuron groups, the lateral-posterior neurons (LPN) and a subset of the dorsal neurons (DN1s), were recently shown to connect the clock network to sleep centers in the fly central complex (Guo et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2016; Lamaze et al., 2018; Ni et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: The DN2 neurons are essential for temperature preference rhythms.
source: The DN2 neurons are essential for temperature preference rhythms (Hamada et al., 2008), whereas no function has so far been assigned to the DN3s.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: No function has so far been assigned to the DN3s.
source: The DN2 neurons are essential for temperature preference rhythms (Hamada et al., 2008), whereas no function has so far been assigned to the DN3s.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge.

claim: All lateral neuron clusters and DN1 dorsal neurons send some of their projections into the accessory medulla.
source: At the anatomical level, all lateral neuron clusters and even DN1 dorsal neurons send some of their projections into the accessory medulla, where they can interact.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: A second area of common interaction is the dorsal brain.
source: A second area of common interaction is the dorsal brain; only the lLNvs do not project there (Helfrich-Förster et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Only the lLNvs do not project to the dorsal brain.
source: A second area of common interaction is the dorsal brain; only the lLNvs do not project there (Helfrich-Förster et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Artificially expressing kinases within specific clock neurons causes their clocks to run fast or slow and changes the overall free-running period of the fly.
source: Artificially expressing kinases within specific clock neurons causes their clocks to run fast or slow and also changes the overall free-running period of the fly, indicating that network signaling adjusts behavior (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Collins et al., 2014; Dissel et al., 2014; Rieger et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2016; Yao and Shafer, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Network signaling adjusts behavior.
source: Artificially expressing kinases within specific clock neurons causes their clocks to run fast or slow and also changes the overall free-running period of the fly, indicating that network signaling adjusts behavior (Chatterjee et al., 2018; Collins et al., 2014; Dissel et al., 2014; Rieger et al., 2006; Yao et al., 2016; Yao and Shafer, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies.

claim: Speeding up or slowing down individual neurons is able to differentially affect behavioral timing in standard light-dark cycles.
source: Similarly, speeding up or slowing down individual neurons is able to differentially affect behavioral timing in standard light-dark (LD) cycles (Stoleru et al., 2005; Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Axons of individual clock cells undergo daily oscillations in their morphology.
source: A high level of neuronal plasticity within the network also exists: axons of individual cells undergo daily oscillations in their morphology (Fernández et al., 2008), and neurons change their targets depending on the environmental condition (Gorostiza et al., 2014; Chatterjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Clock neurons change their targets depending on the environmental condition.
source: A high level of neuronal plasticity within the network also exists: axons of individual cells undergo daily oscillations in their morphology (Fernández et al., 2008), and neurons change their targets depending on the environmental condition (Gorostiza et al., 2014; Chatterjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The core feedback loop consists of several interlocked transcriptional-translational feedback loops.
source: The latter consists of several interlocked transcriptional-translational feedback loops, which probably underlie rhythms in behavior and physiology (Hardin, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The core feedback loop probably underlies rhythms in behavior and physiology.
source: The latter consists of several interlocked transcriptional-translational feedback loops, which probably underlie rhythms in behavior and physiology (Hardin, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: CLK and CYC are transcriptional activators in the core feedback loop.
source: A simplified version of the core feedback loop consists of the transcriptional activators Clock (CLK) and Cycle (CYC) and the transcriptional repressors Period (PER) and Timeless (TIM).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: PER and TIM are transcriptional repressors in the core feedback loop.
source: A simplified version of the core feedback loop consists of the transcriptional activators Clock (CLK) and Cycle (CYC) and the transcriptional repressors Period (PER) and Timeless (TIM).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: CLK and CYC bind to E-boxes within the period and timeless genes and activate their transcription.
source: CLK and CYC bind to E-boxes within the period (per) and timeless (tim) genes (among other clock-controlled genes) and activate their transcription.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: PER and TIM form a heterodimer after synthesis in the cytoplasm.
source: After PER and TIM synthesis in the cytoplasm, they form a heterodimer and enter the nucleus toward the end of the night.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: PER and TIM enter the nucleus toward the end of the night.
source: After PER and TIM synthesis in the cytoplasm, they form a heterodimer and enter the nucleus toward the end of the night.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: PER and TIM interact with CLK and CYC in the nucleus and release them from their E-box targets.
source: There they interact with CLK and CYC, release them from their E-box targets and thereby inhibit their own transcription.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the circadian clock mechanism.

claim: All 75 pairs of clock neurons contain the canonical circadian machinery.
source: All 75 pairs of clock neurons contain this canonical circadian machinery, which undergoes daily oscillations in level.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The canonical circadian machinery undergoes daily oscillations in level.
source: All 75 pairs of clock neurons contain this canonical circadian machinery, which undergoes daily oscillations in level.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The immunohistochemical cycling of PER and TIM within clock neurons is a classic assay to visualize molecular oscillations.
source: Indeed, the immunohistochemical cycling of PER and TIM within these neurons is a classic assay to visualize these molecular oscillations (Menegazzi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Silencing PDF neurons stops their PER cycling.
source: Silencing PDF neurons stops their PER cycling, indicating an important role of neuronal firing in maintaining circadian oscillations.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: PDF neuron silencing phase advances PER cycling in downstream neurons.
source: PDF neuron silencing also phase advances PER cycling in downstream neurons, suggesting that PDF normally serves to delay cycling in target neurons (Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: PDF normally serves to delay cycling in target neurons.
source: PDF neuron silencing also phase advances PER cycling in downstream neurons, suggesting that PDF normally serves to delay cycling in target neurons (Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies.

claim: PDF signaling stabilizes PER.
source: This is consistent with experiments showing that PDF signaling stabilizes PER (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Neuronal activation is able to mimic a light pulse and phase shift the clock due to firing-mediated TIM degradation.
source: In addition, neuronal activation is able to mimic a light pulse and phase shift the clock due to firing-mediated TIM degradation (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Silencing the majority of fly brain clock neurons abolished rhythmic behavior but had no effect on clock protein cycling in LD.
source: Silencing abolished rhythmic behavior but had no effect on clock protein cycling in LD, indicating that the silencing affects circadian output but not oscillator function in a cycling light environment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Silencing affects circadian output but not oscillator function in a cycling light environment.
source: Silencing abolished rhythmic behavior but had no effect on clock protein cycling in LD, indicating that the silencing affects circadian output but not oscillator function in a cycling light environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Silencing abolished rhythmic behavior in DD with very different effects on clock protein cycling.
source: Silencing similarly abolished rhythmic behavior in DD but with very different effects on clock protein cycling.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Protein cycling in the LNds was not affected by neuronal silencing in DD.
source: Although protein cycling in the LNds was not affected by neuronal silencing in DD, the sLNvs dampened almost immediately.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The sLNvs dampened almost immediately upon silencing in DD.
source: Although protein cycling in the LNds was not affected by neuronal silencing in DD, the sLNvs dampened almost immediately.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The differential effect of silencing on different clock neurons is under transcriptional control.
source: Interestingly, this differential effect is under transcriptional control, suggesting that some Drosophila clock neurons experience activity-regulated clock gene transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the tim mRNA data.

claim: Some Drosophila clock neurons experience activity-regulated clock gene transcription.
source: Interestingly, this differential effect is under transcriptional control, suggesting that some Drosophila clock neurons experience activity-regulated clock gene transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the tim mRNA data.

claim: Network properties are critical to maintain wild-type activity-rest rhythms.
source: Cell-specific CRISPR/Cas9 knockouts of the core clock protein PER further suggests that network properties are critical to maintain wild-type activity-rest rhythms.
evidence: This is inferred from the CRISPR knockout experiments.

claim: Clock neuron communication and firing-mediated clock gene transcription are essential for high amplitude and synchronized molecular rhythms as well as rhythmic physiology.
source: Our data taken together show that clock neuron communication and firing-mediated clock gene transcription are essential for high amplitude and synchronized molecular rhythms as well as rhythmic physiology.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both control strains show expected morning and evening anticipation increases in LD cycles.
source: Both control strains show the expected morning and evening (M and E) anticipation increases, which are normal behavioral manifestations of clock function (Figure 1A, C and G).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 1.

claim: There is no discernable activity anticipation in the silenced flies.
source: There is however no discernable activity anticipation in the silenced flies (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 1.

claim: Silenced flies show only brief activity increases precisely at the day/night and night/day transitions.
source: Only brief activity increases are visible, precisely at the day/night and night/day transitions (Figure 1B); these are startle responses (Rieger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 1 and cited from previous literature.

claim: Flies lacking PER show similar behavior to silenced flies in LD.
source: Flies lacking PER show similar behavior (per01 Figure 1D and Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 1.

claim: Adult-specific silencing of PDF neurons significantly advanced the timing of the E peak.
source: We next compared the behavior to flies with silenced PDF neurons. Adult-specific silencing of the PDF neurons using the gene-switch system significantly advanced the timing of the E peak (Figure 1E and F), which reproduces previously published results (Depetris-Chauvin et al., 2011; Nitabach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 1 and cited from previous literature.

claim: Silencing the whole clock neuron network causes a much more severe behavioral phenotype than only silencing the PDF cells.
source: However, the comparison with the clk856 results shown above indicates that silencing the whole clock neuron network causes a much more severe behavioral phenotype than only silencing the PDF cells, that is network silencing completely abolishes rhythmic LD behavior, similar to clock mutant flies.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the behavioral data.

claim: Network silencing completely abolishes rhythmic LD behavior, similar to clock mutant flies.
source: However, the comparison with the clk856 results shown above indicates that silencing the whole clock neuron network causes a much more severe behavioral phenotype than only silencing the PDF cells, that is network silencing completely abolishes rhythmic LD behavior, similar to clock mutant flies.
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data.

claim: PER and PDP1 show robust cycling in LD with PER peaking at the end of the night (ZT0).
source: Both proteins show robust cycling: PER peaks at the end of the night (ZT0), and PDP1 peaks slightly earlier than PER as expected (Hardin, 2011) (Figure 1I–1N).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1.

claim: PDP1 peaks slightly earlier than PER in LD.
source: Both proteins show robust cycling: PER peaks at the end of the night (ZT0), and PDP1 peaks slightly earlier than PER as expected (Hardin, 2011) (Figure 1I–1N).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1 and cited from previous literature.

claim: Network silencing has no detectable effect on clock protein timing or cycling amplitude in LD.
source: This indicates that network silencing has no detectable effect on clock protein timing or cycling amplitude in LD.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1.

claim: Only 17% of the silenced flies were rhythmic in DD.
source: Only 17% of the silenced flies were rhythmic, indicating that network silencing causes high levels of DD arrhythmicity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: Network silencing causes high levels of DD arrhythmicity.
source: Only 17% of the silenced flies were rhythmic, indicating that network silencing causes high levels of DD arrhythmicity (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: 80 percent of the experimental flies were rhythmic at 18°C in the adult-specific silencing experiment.
source: To rule out developmental effects, we applied the tub-GAL80ts system as described above: 80 percent of the experimental flies were rhythmic at 18°C, but they were profoundly arrhythmic at 30°C with only two rhythmic flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Experimental flies were profoundly arrhythmic at 30°C with only two rhythmic flies in the adult-specific silencing experiment.
source: To rule out developmental effects, we applied the tub-GAL80ts system as described above: 80 percent of the experimental flies were rhythmic at 18°C, but they were profoundly arrhythmic at 30°C with only two rhythmic flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adult-specific silencing of only the PDF neurons more weakly reduced rhythmicity.
source: In contrast, adult-specific silencing of only the PDF neurons more weakly reduced rhythmicity (Figure 2A) and also caused a short period (Figure 2B), phenotypes that are essentially indistinguishable from those of the classical pdf01 mutant (Renn et al., 1999).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2 and cited from previous literature.

claim: Adult-specific silencing of only the PDF neurons caused a short period.
source: In contrast, adult-specific silencing of only the PDF neurons more weakly reduced rhythmicity (Figure 2A) and also caused a short period (Figure 2B), phenotypes that are essentially indistinguishable from those of the classical pdf01 mutant (Renn et al., 1999).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2 and cited from previous literature.

claim: All assayed clock neurons from control strains maintain robust and coordinated cycling in DD.
source: As expected, all assayed clock neurons from control strains maintain robust and coordinated cycling in DD (Figure 2C–H); the sLNvs, LNds and DN1s peak slightly sooner than in LD, consistent with the slightly less than 24 hr circadian period in DD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The sLNvs, LNds and DN1s peak slightly sooner in DD than in LD, consistent with the slightly less than 24 hr circadian period in DD.
source: As expected, all assayed clock neurons from control strains maintain robust and coordinated cycling in DD (Figure 2C–H); the sLNvs, LNds and DN1s peak slightly sooner than in LD, consistent with the slightly less than 24 hr circadian period in DD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: Silencing the clock network causes clock protein cycling within the individual neuronal subgroups to differ strongly from each other in amplitude and phase.
source: In striking contrast, silencing the clock network causes clock protein cycling within the individual neuronal subgroups to differ strongly from each other, in amplitude and in phase.
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: Clock protein cycling in the LNds is least affected by neuronal silencing with little to no change in phase or amplitude.
source: Clock protein cycling in the LNds is least affected by neuronal silencing and with little to no change in phase or amplitude, suggesting a robust and possibly self-autonomous clock in these neurons; see Discussion (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The LNds have a robust and possibly self-autonomous clock.
source: Clock protein cycling in the LNds is least affected by neuronal silencing and with little to no change in phase or amplitude, suggesting a robust and possibly self-autonomous clock in these neurons; see Discussion (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The sLNvs dampen and rapidly become arrhythmic upon silencing in DD.
source: The sLNvs in contrast dampen and rapidly become arrhythmic, suggesting that these cells are rather weak oscillators and require network activity or light for proper molecular rhythms (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The sLNvs are rather weak oscillators and require network activity or light for proper molecular rhythms.
source: The sLNvs in contrast dampen and rapidly become arrhythmic, suggesting that these cells are rather weak oscillators and require network activity or light for proper molecular rhythms (Figure 2C and F).
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The DN1s dampen but less strongly than sLNvs and manifest low amplitude cycling which is phase-advanced.
source: The DN1s also dampen but less strongly. They manifest low amplitude cycling, which is phase-advanced; this intermediate situation suggests a fast and somewhat network dependent clock in DN1s (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The DN1s have a fast and somewhat network dependent clock.
source: The DN1s also dampen but less strongly. They manifest low amplitude cycling, which is phase-advanced; this intermediate situation suggests a fast and somewhat network dependent clock in DN1s (Figure 2E and H).
evidence: This is inferred from the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2.

claim: The DN2s were similar to the DN1s in their response to silencing.
source: The DN2s were similar to the DN1s (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on data not shown.

claim: Silencing only the PDF neurons slightly decreased the cycling amplitude in the sLNvs.
source: To compare the contribution of network communication with the release of PDF to PER protein cycling, we also silenced only the PDF neurons in the adult (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). This slightly decreased the cycling amplitude in the sLNvs (p<0.01) but to a much smaller extent than silencing the entire brain clock (p<0.01).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The LNds appeared unaffected by PDF neuron silencing.
source: The LNds appeared unaffected by PDF neuron silencing, whereas the shape but not the amplitude of the PER cycling curve was altered in the DN1s (p=0.1628).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The shape but not the amplitude of the PER cycling curve was altered in the DN1s by PDF neuron silencing.
source: The LNds appeared unaffected by PDF neuron silencing, whereas the shape but not the amplitude of the PER cycling curve was altered in the DN1s (p=0.1628).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PDF contributes to network synchrony but cannot explain all clock protein cycling changes in the clk856>Kir experiments.
source: These data indicate that PDF contributes to network synchrony but cannot explain all clock protein cycling changes in the clk856>Kir experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the PDF neuron silencing and whole network silencing data.

claim: In control flies under LD conditions, tim-RNA cycles robustly in both sLNvs and LNds with a peak toward the beginning of the night.
source: In control flies under LD conditions, tim-RNA cycles robustly in both sLNvs and LNds with a peak toward the beginning of the night as expected.
evidence: This is shown in the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: Clock network silencing had no effect on tim mRNA cycling amplitude or phase in LD.
source: In addition, clock network silencing had no effect on tim mRNA cycling amplitude or phase in LD, which parallels the protein cycling results (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown in the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: In constant darkness (DD5), the controls show robust tim mRNA cycling in both sLNvs and LNds.
source: In constant darkness (DD5), the controls show robust cycling in both sLNvs and LNds as expected, but silencing causes a profound decrease in tim mRNA signal in the sLNvs; the LNds cycle normally (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is shown in the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: Silencing causes a profound decrease in tim mRNA signal in the sLNvs in DD5.
source: In constant darkness (DD5), the controls show robust cycling in both sLNvs and LNds as expected, but silencing causes a profound decrease in tim mRNA signal in the sLNvs; the LNds cycle normally (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is shown in the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: The LNds cycle normally in DD5 after silencing.
source: In constant darkness (DD5), the controls show robust cycling in both sLNvs and LNds as expected, but silencing causes a profound decrease in tim mRNA signal in the sLNvs; the LNds cycle normally (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is shown in the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: The silencing-mediated changes in clock protein cycling are in part transcriptional in origin.
source: These data indicate a direct correlation between neuronal activity and tim RNA levels at least in the sLNvs and suggest that the silencing-mediated changes in clock protein cycling are in part transcriptional in origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: There is a direct correlation between neuronal activity and tim RNA levels at least in the sLNvs.
source: These data indicate a direct correlation between neuronal activity and tim RNA levels at least in the sLNvs and suggest that the silencing-mediated changes in clock protein cycling are in part transcriptional in origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: The PERKO strategy abolished M and E anticipation in LD behavior without affecting the startle responses.
source: This PERKO strategy abolished M and E anticipation in LD behavior without affecting the startle responses (Figure 4C and Figure 4E), and it also reduced the level of DD rhythmicity to below 10%; this reproduced network silencing as well as the canonical per01 behavioral phenotypes (Figures 1D and 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: The PERKO strategy reduced the level of DD rhythmicity to below 10%.
source: This PERKO strategy abolished M and E anticipation in LD behavior without affecting the startle responses (Figure 4C and Figure 4E), and it also reduced the level of DD rhythmicity to below 10%; this reproduced network silencing as well as the canonical per01 behavioral phenotypes (Figures 1D and 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: The PERKO strategy reproduced network silencing as well as the canonical per01 behavioral phenotypes.
source: This PERKO strategy abolished M and E anticipation in LD behavior without affecting the startle responses (Figure 4C and Figure 4E), and it also reduced the level of DD rhythmicity to below 10%; this reproduced network silencing as well as the canonical per01 behavioral phenotypes (Figures 1D and 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: The PERKO strategy works at more than 90% efficiency as determined by the loss of PER immunoreactivity in the lateral neuron clusters.
source: Not surprisingly perhaps given these robust phenotypes, immunohistochemistry indicates that the PERKO strategy works at more than 90% efficiency as determined by the loss of PER immunoreactivity in the lateral neuron clusters of the clk856>Cas9 per-g experiment (Figure 4F–4H).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: There was no detectable nuclear PER signal in all PDF cells or in the DN2s after PERKO.
source: For example, there was no detectable nuclear PER signal in all PDF cells or in the DN2s (Figure 4F and H).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: There is a marked reduction in the number of PER-positive DN1s in the dorsal brain after PERKO.
source: There is also a marked reduction in the number of PER-positive DN1s in the dorsal brain; this is expected as the clk856-GAL4 line does not express in all DN1 neurons (Gummadova et al., 2009) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4 and cited from previous literature.

claim: Most LNds are PER-negative after PERKO, but two LNds remain PER-positive.
source: Similarly, most LNds are PER-negative. There are however two LNds that remain PER-positive for some reason (Figure 4G), that is, there are a few cell escapers.
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: The PERKO with pdf-GAL4 had only a marginal effect on DD rhythmicity compared to the controls.
source: We were therefore surprised that the PERKO with pdf-GAL4 had only a marginal effect on DD rhythmicity compared to the controls (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: A PERKO in the E cells with MB122B-split-GAL4 had no effect on rhythmicity.
source: Similarly, a PERKO in the cells important for controlling E activity (E cells: 3 LNds and the 5th sLNv) with MB122B-split-GAL4 had no effect on rhythmicity (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: A PERKO in both sLNvs and E cells achieved with Mai179-GAL4 lowered rhythmicity to less than 20%.
source: However, a PERKO in both groups achieved with Mai179-GAL4, lowered rhythmicity to less than 20% (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: Knockout in the retina, glial cells or DN1s did not affect rhythmicity.
source: To address whether other neurons have similar effects, we expressed the PER guides elsewhere: knockout in the retina (GMR-GAL4), glial cells (repo-GAL4) or DN1s (clk4.1M-GAL4 and AstC-GAL4) were successful and did not affect rhythmicity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A clock in either of two key places, the sLNvs or the LNds, can drive rhythmic behavior.
source: These findings taken together suggest that a clock in either of two key places, the sLNvs or the LNds, can drive rhythmic behavior.
evidence: This is inferred from the PERKO experiments.

claim: Free-running periods did not change if the PERKO was in the dorsal brain and/or in the large PDF neurons, the lLNvs.
source: These periods did not change if the PERKO was in the dorsal brain and/or in the large PDF neurons, the lLNvs.
evidence: This is shown in the period data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: A PERKO in the E cells and with drivers expressing in these cells plus some dorsal neurons results in a slight but significant period lengthening of approximately 0.5 hr.
source: However, a PERKO in the E cells and with drivers expressing in these cells plus some dorsal neurons results in a slight but significant period lengthening of approximately 0.5 hr.
evidence: This is shown in the period data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: A PERKO in most of the lateral neuron clusters gave rise to a short period.
source: In contrast, a PERKO in most of the lateral neuron clusters gave rise to a short period.
evidence: This is shown in the period data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: The clocks in the two different key neuron subgroups collaborate to achieve the intermediate and close to 24 hr period characteristic of wild-type flies.
source: These two sets of period phenotypes taken together suggest that the clocks in the two different key neuron subgroups collaborate to achieve the intermediate and close to 24 hr period characteristic of wild-type flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the period data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Silencing the clock network in DD causes a damping of molecular oscillations and a drifting apart from the common phase.
source: Silencing the clock network in DD causes a damping of molecular oscillations and a drifting apart from the common phase as indicated by the red waves.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5B.

claim: If network communication is allowed, the different neuronal sub-clusters are mostly in sync and show robust cycling.
source: If network communication is allowed, the different neuronal sub-clusters are mostly in sync and show robust cycling, suggesting neuronal communication is essential for molecular oscillations.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5B.

claim: Neuronal communication is essential for molecular oscillations.
source: If network communication is allowed, the different neuronal sub-clusters are mostly in sync and show robust cycling, suggesting neuronal communication is essential for molecular oscillations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: In a normal LD cycle light drives high amplitude and synchronized cycling even in the absence of neuronal communication.
source: In a normal LD cycle light drives high amplitude and synchronized cycling even in the absence of neuronal communication, establishing a hierarchy of synchronization cues with light on the top.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5B and inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Light is the top synchronization cue in a hierarchy of synchronization cues.
source: In a normal LD cycle light drives high amplitude and synchronized cycling even in the absence of neuronal communication, establishing a hierarchy of synchronization cues with light on the top.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Knocking out core clock components such as period or Clock severely disrupts circadian behavior as well as molecular clock properties in flies and mammals.
source: Knocking out core clock components such as period or Clock severely disrupts circadian behavior as well as molecular clock properties in flies and mammals (Allada et al., 1998; Gekakis et al., 1998; Konopka and Benzer, 1971).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Fly behavior becomes arrhythmic in LD as well as DD conditions when central clock neurons are silenced.
source: Here we show that similar behavioral effects occur when we silence the central clock neurons and thereby abolish communication within this network and with downstream targets, that is fly behavior becomes arrhythmic in LD as well as DD conditions and resembles the phenotypes of core clock mutant strains (Konopka and Benzer, 1971).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rhythmic behavior requires clock neuron output, which is uncoupled from the circadian molecular machinery by network silencing.
source: These findings suggest that 1) rhythmic behavior requires clock neuron output, which is uncoupled from the circadian molecular machinery by network silencing, and 2) synchronized molecular rhythms of clock neurons do not require neuronal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Synchronized molecular rhythms of clock neurons do not require neuronal activity in LD.
source: These findings suggest that 1) rhythmic behavior requires clock neuron output, which is uncoupled from the circadian molecular machinery by network silencing, and 2) synchronized molecular rhythms of clock neurons do not require neuronal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results in LD.

claim: The results presumably reflect the strong effect of the external light-dark cycle on these oscillators.
source: The results presumably reflect the strong effect of the external light-dark cycle on these oscillators.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental results.

claim: In DD, the individual neurons desynchronize and their protein cycling damps to different extents.
source: In DD however, the individual neurons change dramatically: the different neurons desynchronize, and their protein cycling damps to different extents.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: sLNv cycling relies most strongly on neuronal communication.
source: Interestingly, sLNv cycling relies most strongly on neuronal communication: these neurons cycle robustly in controls but apparently not at all in the silenced state.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: sLNvs were previously shown to be essential for DD rhythms.
source: sLNvs were previously shown to be essential for DD rhythms (Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Decreasing the temperature to 18 degrees after a week at high temperature failed to rescue rhythmic behavior.
source: However, a simple interpretation of the adult-specific silencing experiment favors a stopped clock: decreasing the temperature to 18 degrees after a week at high temperature failed to rescue rhythmic behavior.
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A similar experiment in mammals gave rise to the opposite result, suggesting an effect of firing on circadian amplitude in that case.
source: A similar experiment in mammals gave rise to the opposite result, suggesting an effect of firing on circadian amplitude in that case (Yamaguchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Modeling of the clock network suggests that different neurons resynchronize more easily if the most highly-connected cells are intrinsically weak oscillators.
source: In either case, a stopped clock or an effect on clock protein oscillation amplitude, these results make another link to the mammalian literature: modeling of the clock network suggests that different neurons resynchronize more easily if the most highly-connected cells are intrinsically weak oscillators (Webb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The sLNvs are essential for DD rhythms, known to communicate with other clock neurons and are situated in the accessory medulla.
source: The sLNvs are essential for DD rhythms, known to communicate with other clock neurons (Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004) and are situated in the accessory medulla; this is an area of extensive neuronal interactions in many insects (Reischig and Stengl, 2003).
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: The accessory medulla is an area of extensive neuronal interactions in many insects.
source: The sLNvs are essential for DD rhythms, known to communicate with other clock neurons (Grima et al., 2004; Stoleru et al., 2004) and are situated in the accessory medulla; this is an area of extensive neuronal interactions in many insects (Reischig and Stengl, 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: An important role of interneuron communication in DD is in agreement with previous work showing that altering the speed of individual neuron groups can change the phase of downstream target neurons.
source: An important role of interneuron communication in DD is in agreement with previous work showing that altering the speed of individual neuron groups can change the phase of downstream target neurons (Yao and Shafer, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The absence of PDF changes the phase of downstream target neurons.
source: An important signaling molecule is the neuropeptide PDF: its absence changes the phase of downstream target neurons, and silencing PDF neurons causes an essentially identical phenotype to the lack of PDF (Im et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Silencing PDF neurons causes an essentially identical phenotype to the lack of PDF.
source: An important signaling molecule is the neuropeptide PDF: its absence changes the phase of downstream target neurons, and silencing PDF neurons causes an essentially identical phenotype to the lack of PDF (Im et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2004; Wu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The effects of network silencing are much stronger and show different levels of autonomy than PDF ablation.
source: However, the effects reported here are much stronger and show different levels of autonomy than PDF ablation, suggesting that other signaling molecules and/or the neuronal activity of additional clock neurons are essential to maintain proper rhythmic clock protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the experimental results.

claim: Other signaling molecules and/or the neuronal activity of additional clock neurons are essential to maintain proper rhythmic clock protein expression.
source: However, the effects reported here are much stronger and show different levels of autonomy than PDF ablation, suggesting that other signaling molecules and/or the neuronal activity of additional clock neurons are essential to maintain proper rhythmic clock protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: tim mRNA profiles nicely reproduced the protein cycling profiles.
source: Indeed, tim mRNA profiles nicely reproduced the protein cycling profiles: robust cycling of all (assayed) clock neurons was maintained in LD even with silencing, but tim-mRNA levels in the sLNvs stopped cycling in DD; in contrast, robust cycling was maintained in the LNds (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is shown in the FISH data in Figure 3.

claim: The changes in protein cycling amplitude and also possibly phase are under transcriptional control.
source: This suggests that the changes in protein cycling amplitude and also possibly phase are under transcriptional control.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH data.

claim: Neuronal activity promotes clock gene transcription at least in the sLNvs.
source: Importantly, the tim signal in the sLNvs disappeared upon silencing, suggesting that neuronal activity promotes clock gene transcription at least in this subset of neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the FISH data.

claim: This recapitulates for the first time in Drosophila the robust positive relationship between neuronal firing and clock gene transcription in mammals.
source: This recapitulates for the first time in Drosophila the robust positive relationship between neuronal firing and clock gene transcription in mammals (Shigeyoshi et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding and cited from mammalian literature.

claim: Drosophila neuronal firing had only been connected to post-transcriptional clock protein regulation, namely TIM degradation.
source: To date, Drosophila neuronal firing had only been connected to post-transcriptional clock protein regulation, namely TIM degradation (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: TIM degradation might be required to relieve transcriptional repression and maintain cycling.
source: Conceivably, these two effects are connected: TIM degradation might be required to relieve transcriptional repression and maintain cycling.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental results.

claim: The cell-specific knockout strategy worked reliably and specifically, in glial cells as well as neurons, with high efficiency and with no apparent background effects.
source: This adult brain knockout strategy worked reliably and specifically, in glial cells as well as neurons, with high efficiency and with no apparent background effects (Figure 4B–G).
evidence: This is shown in the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4.

claim: Expression of the guides with the clk856-GAL4 driver phenocopied per01 behavior.
source: Importantly, expression of the guides with the clk856-GAL4 driver phenocopied per01 behavior (Figure 4C and H).
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: PERKO in the PDF cells did not increase the level of arrhythmicity.
source: PERKO in the PDF cells did not increase the level of arrhythmicity, only a PERKO in most lateral neurons, E cells as well as PDF cells, generated high levels of arrhythmic behavior.
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: Only a PERKO in most lateral neurons, E cells as well as PDF cells, generated high levels of arrhythmic behavior.
source: PERKO in the PDF cells did not increase the level of arrhythmicity, only a PERKO in most lateral neurons, E cells as well as PDF cells, generated high levels of arrhythmic behavior.
evidence: This is shown in the behavioral data in Figure 4.

claim: Previous rescue or knockdown experiments suggested per rescue in all neurons except the PDF neurons did not restore wildtype behavior.
source: This result is surprising given previous rescue or knockdown experiments (Herrero et al., 2017; Stoleru et al., 2004): per rescue in all neurons except the PDF neurons (elav-GAL4 pdf-GAL80) did not restore wildtype behavior.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The rescue significantly improved the rhythmicity index compared to control flies.
source: However, this rescue significantly improved the rhythmicity index compared to control flies, which can be interpreted as lower rhythm power, a feature we also observed in our pdf PERKO.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The guide strategy appears to be superior to knockdown experiments.
source: From this point of view, the guide strategy appears to be superior; it mutates DNA sequences and should be more robust to differences in expression strength.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the PERKO results with previous knockdown experiments.

claim: Ablating the PDF cells causes high levels of arrhythmicity.
source: Even though a clock in the PDF neurons appears to be dispensable for rhythmicity, the cell bodies still appear essential. This is because ablating the PDF cells causes high levels of arrhythmicity (Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The LNds can drive the rhythmic output of key sLNv genes like PDF even in the absence of a clock in these neurons.
source: The data shown here therefore suggest that the LNds can drive the rhythmic output of key sLNv genes like PDF even in the absence of a clock in these neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the PERKO experiments.

claim: The LNds project dendritic as well as axonal arborizations into the accessory medulla, the location of the sLNvs.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, recent data indicate that the LNds project dendritic as well as axonal arborizations into the accessory medulla, the location of the sLNvs, indicating extensive communication between these two important subgroups of clock neurons (Schlichting et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: Ablating per in the LNds causes a long period.
source: This interpretation is further supported by examining the free-running period of the cell-specific knockouts: Ablating per in the LNds causes a long period, whereas ablating PER in most lateral clock neurons causes a short period phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in the period data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Ablating PER in most lateral clock neurons causes a short period phenotype.
source: This interpretation is further supported by examining the free-running period of the cell-specific knockouts: Ablating per in the LNds causes a long period, whereas ablating PER in most lateral clock neurons causes a short period phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in the period data in Figure 5 and Table 1.

claim: Interactions between the sLNvs and other clock cells, perhaps within the accessory medulla, are essential for the close to 24 hr speed of the overall brain and behavioral clock.
source: These data suggest that interactions between the sLNvs and other clock cells, perhaps within the accessory medulla, are essential for the close to 24 hr speed of the overall brain and behavioral clock.
evidence: This is inferred from the period data.

claim: A second study similarly highlights the dependence of DD rhythms on network properties.
source: The second study is recently published and similarly highlights the dependence of DD rhythms on network properties (Bulthuis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: Bulthuis et al. report a decrease in rhythmicity upon knockout of the circadian clock in PDF cells.
source: However, they report a decrease in rhythmicity upon knockout of the circadian clock in PDF cells, an effect that neither we nor Delventhal observed.
evidence: This is cited from recent literature.

claim: The difference in results may be due to the knockout strategy used by Bulthuis et al., namely overexpression of a dominant negative Cycle isoform within PDF cells.
source: This difference may be due to their knockout strategy, namely, overexpression of a dominant negative Cycle isoform within PDF cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on comparing different experimental approaches.

claim: The dominant negative Cycle protein may have effects on gene expression beyond knocking out the circadian clock.
source: This protein may have effects on gene expression beyond knocking out the circadian clock.
evidence: This is speculated based on the nature of the experimental approach.

claim: The conceptually simpler PERKO strategy has fewer side effects and is therefore superior.
source: The distinction furthermore suggests that the conceptually simpler PERKO strategy has fewer side effects and is therefore superior.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing different experimental approaches.

claim: Some of the communication properties described here resemble what has been found in mammalian systems.
source: Some of the communication properties described here resemble what has been found in mammalian systems.
evidence: This is stated based on comparing the results with mammalian literature.

claim: Decreasing neuronal interactions by creating sparse SCN cultures changes the free-running period and activity phase of individual neurons.
source: For example, decreasing neuronal interactions by creating sparse SCN cultures changes the free-running period and activity phase of individual neurons (Welsh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Communication is critical for circadian phase and period determination in mammals.
source: This suggests that communication is also critical for circadian phase and period determination in mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from cited mammalian studies.

claim: Fly clock cells may be even less cell-autonomous and more dependent on communication than what has been described for mammals.
source: Nonetheless, fly clock cells may be even less cell-autonomous and more dependent on communication than what has been described for mammals (reviewed in Evans, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results with mammalian literature.

claim: The fly system may be particularly dependent on light.
source: First, the fly system may be particularly dependent on light.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and comparison with mammalian systems.

claim: Peripheral fly clocks appear strongly light-dependent in contrast to what has been described for mammalian liver.
source: For example, peripheral fly clocks appear strongly light-dependent in contrast to what has been described for mammalian liver (reviewed in Ito and Tomioka, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Circadian cycling in the periphery crashes rapidly under constant darkness conditions.
source: Although much of the fly data could reflect cellular asynchrony in constant darkness, circadian cycling in the periphery crashes rapidly under these conditions and resembles the strong and rapid non-cycling that occurs in the sLNvs upon silencing in DD.
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge.

claim: Fly cryptochrome but not mammalian cryptochrome is light-sensitive.
source: Notably, fly cryptochrome but not mammalian cryptochrome is light-sensitive (reviewed in Michael et al., 2017) and probably contributes to the light-dependence of fly peripheral clocks.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Light can directly penetrate the thin insect cuticle.
source: This is also because light can directly penetrate the thin insect cuticle, which probably contributes to making the fly brain less dependent on ocular photoreception than the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Some fly clock neurons do not express cryptochrome.
source: However, some fly clock neurons do not express cryptochrome, suggesting that the fly clock system is dependent on network interactions even in a light-dark cycle (Benito et al., 2008; Yoshii et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The fly clock system is dependent on network interactions even in a light-dark cycle.
source: However, some fly clock neurons do not express cryptochrome, suggesting that the fly clock system is dependent on network interactions even in a light-dark cycle (Benito et al., 2008; Yoshii et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies.

claim: The fly circadian network is an attractive object of study because of its limited size of 75 neuron pairs.
source: These considerations suggest that the fly circadian network is an attractive object of study not only because of its limited size of 75 neuron pairs but also because of its strong dependence on neuronal communication.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the discussion.

claim: The fly circadian network is an attractive object of study because of its strong dependence on neuronal communication.
source: These considerations suggest that the fly circadian network is an attractive object of study not only because of its limited size of 75 neuron pairs but also because of its strong dependence on neuronal communication.
